concept.name: Treasury note
concept.definition: A U.S. Treasury marketable security issued with maturities of 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years. Notes pay interest every six months and repay the face value at maturity.
concept.intuition: A Treasury note is the middle of the government yield curve: multi-year lending to the U.S. government with a steady semiannual coupon.
concept.mechanics: Notes are auctioned on a regular schedule, pay a fixed coupon semiannually, and trade in one of the world's deepest secondary markets. The 10-year note's yield is a global benchmark for mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, and asset valuation discount rates.
concept.failure_modes: Notes carry duration risk: prices fall when yields rise, roughly in proportion to maturity. Inflation erodes the real value of the fixed coupons, and sellers before maturity receive the market price, not face value.
concept.misconceptions: That a Treasury note cannot lose money — its market price fluctuates daily, and an investor who sells after yields rise realizes a loss. Safety of principal applies only when held to maturity, in nominal terms.
concept.example: A 5-year Treasury note with a 4% coupon pays $20 every six months per $1,000 of face value and returns the $1,000 at maturity.
